intro:
These exercises drill the chapter's central decision: pick the narrowest contiguous-storage shape that the workload's semantics actually require. Arrays carry a compile-time length as part of their type; slices borrow a contiguous view without owning the allocation; vectors own a growable heap buffer. The skill being built is reading a workload's ownership, size invariant, mutation pattern, and locality needs, then mapping those to `[T; N]`, `&[T]`, or `Vec<T>` without resorting to habit or folklore.

The later exercises push the same model into operational territory: reading `len` versus `capacity`, writing algorithms against slices so callers keep storage control, measuring whether preallocation matters instead of assuming it, and repairing a borrow that outlived a structural mutation. The lab is the concrete payoff: a single `&[u32]` function that serves an array subslice and a vector subslice with no allocation and no narrower public signature.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose array, slice, vector, or inline-first storage from the workload
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Work from invariants first, performance last. The four cases map cleanly once you separate API shape from storage shape.

The 16-byte protocol header has a compile-time fixed length that is part of the invariant: a header is exactly 16 bytes, not "usually about 16." That is `[u8; 16]`. Putting the length in the type means `[u8; 16]` and `[u8; 20]` are different types, so a miscounted field is a compile error rather than a runtime surprise, and the value can live inline in a struct with no heap allocation.

The read-only checksum helper only needs a borrowed view over whatever bytes the caller already owns. It should take `&[u8]` (or `&mut [u8]` if it scribbles a running state into a caller-provided buffer). A slice parameter lets the same helper run over an array, a vector, or a subslice without forcing the caller to allocate or surrender ownership. The helper has no business deciding the caller's storage strategy.

The dynamically accumulated retry batch genuinely needs owned growth: the count is not known ahead of time and the batch must outlive the function that fills it. That is `Vec<T>`. If you can derive a trustworthy upper bound (for example, the batch can never exceed the number of input jobs), `Vec::with_capacity` is justified, but the storage choice itself is driven by owned, unbounded growth.

The tiny hot list of usually three tags is the only case that might justify an inline-first (small-vector) representation, and only after profiling. The common-path size is small and the structure may be created in large numbers, so spilling to the heap on the rare large case while keeping the common case inline can pay off. But that is a measured optimization, not a default: inline-first containers enlarge the parent struct and raise move cost, so a plain `Vec<T>` (or even `[T; N]` plus a length if three is a hard cap) is the honest starting point until a profile shows allocation is the real cost.
criteria: Fixed-size case (16-byte header) maps to `[u8; 16]` because the length is a semantic invariant baked into the type.
Read-only checksum helper takes `&[u8]`/`&mut [u8]` so it borrows the caller's contiguous data without owning it.
Retry batch is `Vec<T>` because growth is unbounded and the batch must outlive the filling function.
Inline-first storage for the tag list is named as profile-conditional, not adopted as a default style.

exerciseSolutions.title: Read `len` and `capacity` operationally
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The helper allocates capacity for 1024 elements up front, pushes 600, then logs both numbers. Reading them operationally: after 600 pushes, `len()` is 600 and `capacity()` is 1024.

`len()` is occupancy. It is the exact count of logically present, initialized elements the vector is currently holding. It is the bound that indexing and iteration respect: valid indices are `0..len`, and `iter()` yields exactly `len` items. It says nothing about allocation; it only counts what is actually there right now.

`capacity()` is allocation slack. It is the number of elements the current heap buffer can hold before the vector must allocate a larger buffer and move its elements. With `with_capacity(1024)` and 600 pushes, the next 424 pushes can proceed without reallocation, because `len + 1 <= capacity` still holds. Capacity is a budget, not a count of present elements; the elements between index 600 and 1024 are uninitialized backing storage, not logical elements.

`capacity() == 1024` is not a portable design assumption for every vector in the system because capacity is an implementation-controlled property, not a language guarantee. This vector reports 1024 only because someone explicitly requested it with `with_capacity(1024)` and 600 pushes stayed under that budget. A vector built with `Vec::new()` and grown by pushing follows the standard library's internal growth strategy, which Rust deliberately does not pin in its contract. Hard-coding an expected capacity, or relying on a specific growth factor to back into one, encodes folklore as if it were a guarantee. The correct contract is: `capacity() >= len()` always, and the exact surplus is an implementation detail you validate by measurement, not by assumption.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: len() counts present elements; capacity() is the pre-reallocation budget; only capacity() >= len() is guaranteed.
criteria: `len()` is explained as the count of logically present, initialized elements.
`capacity()` is explained as the allocation budget available before the next growth/reallocation step.
The answer rejects relying on an exact capacity or growth factor as a correctness assumption and keeps only `capacity() >= len()` as the contract.

exerciseSolutions.title: Write the function over slices, not vectors
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The algorithm only needs to read a contiguous run of `u32` values and reduce them to a sum. It has no reason to own anything, decide an allocation strategy, or know whether the data came from an array or a vector. So the parameter stays exactly `&[u32]`, a borrowed contiguous view.

The reduction is one line: `values.iter().copied().sum()`. `iter()` yields `&u32`, `copied()` turns each `&u32` into a `u32` (cheap, because `u32: Copy`), and `sum()` reduces them. No new vector is allocated; the function reads through the borrow and returns a scalar. An explicit `for` loop accumulating into a `u32` would be equally valid and compile to essentially the same code.

The payoff is exactly what a slice-first signature buys. In the lab, `&fixed[2..5]` borrows three elements out of a stack array and `&dynamic[..3]` borrows three elements out of a heap-backed vector. Both convert to `&[u32]` at the call site with no copy and no allocation, so the function serves both owners through one signature. Because the function never names `Vec<u32>`, it imposes no ownership constraint on callers: arrays, vector borrows, and arbitrary subslices all flow through unchanged. `&fixed[2..5]` is `[15, 16, 23]` which sums to 54, and `&dynamic[..3]` is `[3, 6, 9]` which sums to 18, matching the lab's expected output.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: A reduction over a borrowed &[u32] — works for any contiguous source without allocating.
criteria: Signature stays exactly `fn window_sum(values: &[u32]) -> u32`.
Returns 54 for `&fixed[2..5]` (15+16+23) and 18 for `&dynamic[..3]` (3+6+9), as required by the lab.
Reads through the borrow and returns a scalar, never allocating or owning a `Vec<u32>`.

exerciseSolutions.title: Benchmark preallocation versus push-only growth honestly
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The honest way to compare `Vec::new()` against `Vec::with_capacity(n)` is to push the identical workload into each, many times, in release mode, and report what you observe rather than what you expect. The harness below pushes `n` `u64` values into each variant, repeats the whole thing for several iterations to dampen noise, sums per-strategy wall-clock time, and records the final capacity of each.

Two correctness points matter for the benchmark to mean anything. First, the pushed element type and the loop shape are identical between the two variants, so the only difference under test is the allocation strategy. Second, `std::hint::black_box` is applied to the pushed value and the finished vector so the optimizer cannot delete the loop or hoist the work out; without that, a release build can optimize a pure push-and-drop loop into nothing and the measurement becomes meaningless.

What you typically observe: the `Vec::new()` variant grows through a sequence of reallocations and ends at a capacity at least `n` but usually larger than `n` (the standard library overshoots to amortize growth), while the `with_capacity(n)` variant performs exactly one allocation and ends at capacity `n`. The timing difference depends entirely on `n` and on what `T` is. For large `n` or for elements whose moves are non-trivial, preallocation visibly reduces time because it removes repeated reallocate-and-copy steps. For small `n` it can be in the noise. The reportable tradeoff is this: `with_capacity` adds a planning step and a real, named upper bound to your code, and it pays off only when the bound is genuine and the allocation churn it removes is actually on a hot path. A toy microbenchmark validates the direction of the effect; it does not by itself justify a production change, because real workloads interleave other allocations and cache traffic that a tight loop does not model.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Identical workload under two allocation strategies; black_box prevents elision; reports timing and final capacity.
criteria: The harness pushes the same `u64` workload with the same loop into both `Vec::new()` and `Vec::with_capacity(n)`, isolating allocation strategy as the only variable.
Noise is reduced via repeated iterations, release-mode intent, and `black_box` to defeat dead-code elimination.
Results are framed as observations (capacity logs plus timing) rather than an assumption that preallocation always wins.
The tradeoff is named: `with_capacity` adds a planning step tied to a real bound, and only pays off when the removed allocation churn is on a hot path.

exerciseSolutions.title: Repair a slice borrow that outlives its backing vector's mutation
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect is not compiler stubbornness; it is a slice held across a structural mutation of the storage it views. `let hot = &buffer[..4];` borrows a view into the vector's current heap buffer. `buffer.push(99)` may grow the vector, which can reallocate to a larger buffer and move the elements, leaving `hot` pointing at storage that no longer belongs to the live data. A slice is a view into existing storage, not a durable reservation of future layout, so reading from `hot` after the push is reading a stale view. The borrow checker rejects this precisely because `push` takes `&mut buffer` while `hot` still holds a shared borrow, and that conflict is the language refusing to let a view outlive the layout it was taken against.

There are two honest repairs, chosen by whether the code truly needs that data after the push.

If the borrowed work can simply happen first, do it first and let the borrow end before the mutation. Two phases make the lifetimes trivial to review: consume `hot` (compute whatever sum or check you needed), then mutate the buffer. Non-lexical lifetimes end the borrow at its last use, so once `hot` is no longer read, `push` is free to grow the buffer. No copy is needed; the work is just reordered.

If later code genuinely needs that tiny fixed header after the structural change, copy the small, truly-needed subset into independent storage on purpose. Copying four `u32` values into a `[u32; 4]` array detaches them from the vector's buffer entirely, so any subsequent `push` and reallocation cannot invalidate them. This is the honest version of "keep the header": you are not pretending a view survived growth, you are deliberately taking ownership of a fixed copy. The array also encodes the real invariant (exactly four header words) in its type. Do not reach for `clone()` of the whole vector or for raw pointers to dodge the borrow; both restate the bug instead of fixing it.

The two repairs are shown as separately named functions (`two_phase` and `copy_then_grow`) only for clarity, so each path can be read on its own; the point is not a particular signature. The fix is that the borrow must end before the push, regardless of what the caller-visible API ends up looking like, so you are free to keep the original name and return type if that is what the surrounding code needs.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Either end the borrow before mutating (two phases) or deliberately copy the fixed header into an owned [u32; 4].
criteria: The repair ends the active borrow before `push` (two-phase form) or copies the needed four elements into an owned `[u32; 4]`.
The failure is explained as borrowing a view into storage that growth may reallocate and move, not as compiler obstinance.
The original `hot` slice is never read across the vector's growth path in either variant.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose the right contiguous-storage design for three real workloads
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Each subsystem gets one concrete representation, justified by its operational shape, not by type-name preference.

The packet parser with fixed headers wants arrays. A protocol header is a semantically fixed bound: a given header is exactly N bytes by specification. Represent each fixed field as `[u8; N]` (for example a `[u8; 4]` length-prefix or a `[u8; 16]` address). The size lives in the type, so a field-width mistake is a compile error, the header can sit inline inside a parsed-frame struct with no heap allocation, and parsing a frame does not touch the allocator at all on the header path. Arrays here are about correctness of the invariant first and zero-allocation locality second.

The metrics engine that scans rolling numeric windows wants slice-first APIs. The caller already owns the sample buffer (often a ring buffer or a `Vec<f64>` the engine maintains), so the scanning functions should take `&[f64]` and compute over a borrowed window such as `&samples[start..end]`. This is also the locality argument: a contiguous slice of numeric samples is exactly the layout a windowed scan wants, because sequential reads stream through cache lines with predictable prefetching, and the algorithm never copies the window just to read it. Slice-first keeps the engine free to change how it stores samples without rewriting every scan.

The request pipeline that accumulates retryable jobs wants owned vectors. The count of retryable jobs is not known up front and the accumulated batch must outlive the function that builds it, so it returns a `Vec<Job>`. Preallocation is justified here by a real upper bound, not a guess: the retry batch can never contain more jobs than the input it filters, so `Vec::with_capacity(input.len())` reserves once from a genuine bound and then the loop only filters and pushes, removing reallocation churn from the accumulation path. That is exactly the pattern the chapter's capacity example uses.

Would any subsystem justify an inline-first representation? Possibly the metrics engine, if it creates many tiny per-key scratch buffers whose common size is a handful of samples. But that stays a measured optimization: it would have to be proven by a profile showing that allocation of those small buffers is a real cost, weighed against the larger struct size and higher move cost an inline-first container imposes. Absent that measurement, plain `Vec` is the correct default, and inline-first remains a conditional answer rather than a stylistic one.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Arrays for fixed headers, slice-first scans for borrowed windows, preallocated owned Vec for the bounded retry batch.
criteria: Each subsystem gets one named representation justified by workload shape: `[u8; N]` arrays for fixed headers, `&[f64]` slices for the metrics scan, owned `Vec` for the retry batch.
Locality is discussed for the metrics engine: contiguous numeric windows stream through cache lines under a slice-first scan.
The retry-batch preallocation is justified by a real upper bound (result cannot exceed the input length), not a guessed capacity.
Inline-first storage is kept as a measurement-gated optimization for the small-scratch case, not adopted as a default style.

labSolution.explanation:
The only change from the starter is the body of `window_sum`. The starter returned `values[0]`, which read just the first element; the fix reduces the entire borrowed window with `values.iter().copied().sum()`. `iter()` yields `&u32`, `copied()` dereferences each to a `u32` (cheap because `u32: Copy`), and `sum()` folds them into the returned scalar. The function never allocates and never owns a vector; it reads straight through the `&[u32]` borrow.

The two call sites show why the slice parameter is the right contract. `&fixed[2..5]` borrows indices 2, 3, and 4 of the stack array `[4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42]`, which are `15`, `16`, and `23`; their sum is `54`. `&dynamic[..3]` borrows indices 0, 1, and 2 of the heap-backed vector `[3, 6, 9, 12]`, which are `3`, `6`, and `9`; their sum is `18`. Both an array subslice and a vector subslice coerce to `&[u32]` with no copy and no allocation, so one function serves both owners.

The program therefore prints `fixed = 54` then `dynamic = 18`, matching the expected output exactly. The lesson the lab makes concrete is the chapter's slice-first rule: because the algorithm only needs a contiguous read-only view, the signature borrows a slice and leaves every storage decision to the caller.

reviewAnswers.question: When is `[T; N]` the right type rather than `Vec<T>`?
reviewAnswers.answer: Use `[T; N]` when the length is a compile-time invariant that is part of the data's meaning, such as a fixed protocol header, a coordinate triple, or a fixed-width cryptographic value. The count lives in the type, so `[u8; 4]` and `[u8; 8]` are distinct types and a wrong size is a compile error rather than a runtime bug, and the value can live inline with no heap allocation. Reach for `Vec<T>` instead only when the count is genuinely runtime-determined or the collection must grow.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is `&[T]` usually a better function parameter than `&Vec<T>`?
reviewAnswers.answer: `&[T]` borrows a contiguous view without caring who owns the storage, so the same function accepts an array, a vector borrow, or an arbitrary subslice with no allocation and no narrower signature. `&Vec<T>` leaks an allocation assumption the algorithm almost never needs: it forces the caller to have a `Vec` specifically and exposes capacity and growth concerns the function does not use. Taking a slice keeps the API honest about what it actually requires (contiguous read access) and keeps callers in control of their own storage choices.

reviewAnswers.question: What is the practical difference between `len()` and `capacity()`?
reviewAnswers.answer: `len()` is occupancy: the exact count of logically present, initialized elements, and the bound that indexing and iteration respect. `capacity()` is allocation slack: how many elements the current heap buffer can hold before the vector must reallocate to a larger buffer and move its elements. The only guaranteed relationship is `capacity() >= len()`; the surplus is an implementation detail, so you push without reallocation exactly while `len() + pushes <= capacity()`.

reviewAnswers.question: Why should production code avoid depending on a specific vector growth factor?
reviewAnswers.answer: Rust does not promise any particular growth factor in its language contract; the growth strategy is an implementation detail the standard library is free to change. Code that hard-codes an expected capacity, or back-calculates one from an assumed doubling factor, encodes folklore as if it were a guarantee and can silently break when the implementation changes. The portable contract is only `capacity() >= len()`, so when capacity matters you should request it explicitly with `with_capacity`/`reserve` and validate behavior with measurements, capacity logs, or allocation tracing rather than assumption.

reviewAnswers.question: What workload characteristics make contiguous storage especially attractive?
reviewAnswers.answer: Contiguous storage shines when you scan or reduce many elements in sequence, because sequential access streams through cache lines with predictable prefetching, giving strong locality that pointer-chasing structures cannot match. It also keeps the owner value tiny, three words for a vector, so moving or returning the collection transfers ownership of the buffer without copying the elements. Workloads like numeric window scans, parsing, hashing, and serialization, which read or transform runs of elements in order, benefit most, and a slice over that contiguous memory expresses exactly the access pattern those algorithms need.

reviewAnswers.question: When would you choose `iter_mut()` over `into_iter()` on a `Vec<T>`?
reviewAnswers.answer: Choose `iter_mut()` when you want to rewrite the existing elements in place and keep the same vector afterward: it yields `&mut T`, mutates the buffer the vector already owns, and leaves the collection intact for further use. Choose `into_iter()` only when you are done with the vector as a container and want to take ownership of each element by value, for example to move them into another structure or to consume them; it yields `T` and consumes the vector. So the deciding question is ownership of the result: `iter_mut()` updates and preserves the vector, while `into_iter()` tears it down to hand you the elements. Rebuilding a brand-new `Vec<T>` just to change values in place is wasteful when `iter_mut()` edits the existing buffer with no allocation.

reviewAnswers.question: When does `split_at_mut` let you write to two parts of a slice at the same time?
reviewAnswers.answer: `split_at_mut(mid)` splits one mutable slice into two non-overlapping mutable subslices, `&mut [..mid]` and `&mut [mid..]`, and because the borrow checker can prove the two halves do not alias, you may hold and write through both at once. This is what you reach for when an algorithm reads or writes one region while updating another, such as copying from a source half into a destination half or updating a window in terms of its neighbors, which a single `&mut [T]` borrow would otherwise forbid because two overlapping mutable borrows of the same slice are not allowed. The guarantee holds only because the two pieces are disjoint by construction; it is not a way to alias the same elements mutably.
